recentes.titreEditorial: More than twenty countries call for stronger human oversight of AI, without the United States, China or France, while Washington and Beijing open a warning channel between them ahead of the Trump-Xi summit. Google launches its Googlebook at $899 to sell Gemini, Meta's Muse agent races to the top of the charts before being blocked by Amazon and flagged for a security flaw, and British Columbia sues OpenAI after a mass shooting.

Charles III gathers AI bosses in Scotland and warns of \"existential dangers\", while a Pew survey across 37 countries shows a worldwide fear of job destruction. Brussels adopts the EU KIDS Act, Mistral moves into Firefox, Nvidia, Google and Anthropic join forces to find 100 gigawatts on the power grid, and Huawei pulls its next training chip forward by nine months to close the gap with Nvidia.

OpenAI admits six model misbehaviours and publishes a framework to report them, the same day Google opens the connected home to agents and Anthropic folds its interfaces into a single Claude that decides for itself how much work to take on. The agent moves from reading to acting. Meanwhile Brussels adopts the EU KIDS Act to keep minors off social media, Mistral arrives in Firefox, and Huawei pulls its next AI chip nine months forward to cut China's dependence on Nvidia.
Silicon Valley refuses to brake, Washington splits
AI leaders' call to slow down splits the world

AI leaders call for slowing the race, the White House refuses: Dario Amodei argues for \"pacing the frontier\", Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis agree, Donald Trump replies that he will not hand his lead to China, and Asian markets fall. Anthropic is eyeing the Nasdaq for a listing that could exceed $86 billion while OpenAI backs away from its own, SoftBank borrows $11.9 billion to fund OpenAI and Christine Lagarde warns about the financial cost of AI. In China, Z.ai returns to raise $5 billion in Hong Kong and the intelligence chief warns about the risks of AI.

AI safety moves from the activist fringe to mainstream debate: Sam Altman says he is ready to slow frontier AI development and is testing whether such a brake would be legal, a former Anthropic researcher warns that \"AI could kill us all,\" OpenAI adds a worried researcher to its board, and Anthropic publishes 161 pages of Claude misuse, from Yemeni missiles to fake dating profiles. In Europe, the CNIL sets rules for electronic invoicing and the EU's cybersecurity agency trials Anthropic's most offensive model. In China, DeepSeek reignites the price war with its V4.1 Flash model and chipmaker Enflame jumps 188% on its stock market debut. Microsoft plans 38 gigawatts of data centres and Jensen Huang promises Nvidia 70% growth.
Apple's first Ternus keynote and the OECD's student warning
OpenAI claims a Navier-Stokes proof, then a credit fight erupts

Mistral AI raises €3 billion at a €21 billion valuation in a round led by Samsung; the labor-law scholar Jean-Emmanuel Ray reminds employers that the AI Act requires them to inventory their high-risk AI systems and inform staff by the end of 2027, while BPCE stands up its AI Factory and Bercy renegotiates the French state's IT contracts; China targets 9,800 eflops of compute and Huawei launches its first stacked-circuit chip; Revolut completes the first AI-initiated payment in France

Moody's finds that Chinese companies get more compute per dollar spent than the US giants; the Seattle Times and Newsday sue OpenAI and Microsoft over copyright while the split of the Anthropic settlement pits authors against publishers; Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI's chief scientist, describes an alien mind and calls for guardrails; and US job seekers hide instructions in their resumes to trick recruiters' AI
OpenAI ships GPT-6 Astra as three assistants go dark
Washington backs OpenAI against the New York Times
OpenAI rates Astra at critical cyber capability

The European Commission ranks ChatGPT among its most closely watched services under the DSA, the first generative AI targeted, OpenAI moves some of its large customers to performance-based billing, Anthropic signs $35 billion in compute with Lambda ahead of its IPO, and Nvidia invests $3.5 billion in MediaTek to stay indispensable

Sony Music and Warner sue Anthropic for \"one of the largest thefts of intellectual property in history\" on the eve of its stock market listing, Bill Gates calls for taxing machines, Google rolls out its AI answers by default at the expense of the blue links, and Caterpillar applies thirty years of mining automation to AI

Nvidia moves on Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, the open-source platform founded by three French entrepreneurs, the same week it was breached by OpenAI's agents; a federal judge overturns the Pentagon's ban on Anthropic, OpenAI brings advertising to ChatGPT in India, Zhipu unveils an open model trained on 100,000 Chinese chips, and OpenAI documents what critical thinking changes about using a chatbot

Nvidia posts a record $96.2 billion in quarterly revenue and looks ahead to 2028, while Amazon triples its chip order and Anthropic signs $45 billion of compute with Nscale; on the same day, OpenAI releases its report on the Hugging Face breach carried out by nearly 700 of its own agents, Bill Gates breaks his silence to call for a robot tax, and the CNIL updates its open-model traceability tool
Open-weight models pass proprietary ones on Vercel
Uber fined €825 million over automated decisions

Nvidia warns its biggest customers of a price rise above 15% on its AI servers as memory costs soar; the same day SoftBank places a record bond to fund OpenAI, Samsung returns $79 billion under the pressure of the AI boom, Alibaba raises $10.2 billion in Hong Kong, and Hugging Face is said to be exploring a sale at around $13 billion
Anthropic eyes a SpaceX-sized listing as enterprise buyers switch models
The AI Act makes provenance a job
OpenAI freezes part of Astra over cyber risk
Jeff Dean leaves Google as DeepMind reshuffles its command

une.titre: More than twenty countries call for stronger human oversight of AI, without the sector's three great powers
une.texteHtml: The leaders of some twenty countries, including Germany and Canada, along with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, have signed a joint declaration calling for humans to stay in control, Le Monde reports. The text reflects a concern now shared at the highest levels of government: AI development could outpace our ability to keep it in check. The most telling absence is that of the missing signatories. The United States, China and France, three leading powers in the field, did not add their names. The dividing line is sharp between those betting on coordinated safeguards and those keeping their hands free, each for different reasons. A declaration without the players building the most advanced models works above all as a political signal.

items.titre: Article 4 of the AI Act, rewritten, tightens the AI training obligation for SMEs
items.texteHtml: Since 27 July 2026, the European regulation no longer asks for a "sufficient level" of AI literacy among employees, but the obligation to act remains fully in force, the Journal du Net analyses. For an SME, the practical question is no longer ticking a compliance box, it is proving that its teams know how to use the tools it deploys and understand their limits.

items.titre: Google commits €13 billion in Finland, its largest European investment
items.texteHtml: The sum, planned by 2028, will fund data centres built to absorb global AI demand, ZDNet reports, describing a Finland on its way to becoming a Nordic computing hub. The choice follows low-carbon electricity and a cold climate, two assets for cooling server rooms, and confirms that Europe's AI battle is fought as much over land and energy as over models.

items.titre: Retailers launch a race to avoid being bypassed by ChatGPT
items.texteHtml: To preserve their online presence, brands are building their own shopping agents and trying to improve their visibility in AI engines, Le Monde describes. The stakes are concrete: when a customer asks an assistant for advice rather than a search engine, the brand missing from the answer drops out of view at the moment of decision.

items.titre: Google launches its Googlebook at $899, a bet on the appetite for a computer built for Gemini
items.texteHtml: The US giant unveils a range of laptops where Gemini is stitched into the system: the model is wired to the cursor, dictation, widgets and settings, TechCrunch describes. These machines merge Android and ChromeOS and target the premium market held by Apple's MacBook and Windows PCs. Sameer Samat, president of the Android ecosystem, embraces the pairing with the phone, in the manner of the continuity between the iPhone and the Mac. The bet is clear: convince a user to buy a new device for the assistant that lives on it rather than for raw power. Google had failed to make the Chromebook a mainstream success, and it is trying again with AI as the central argument.

items.titre: Meta's Muse agent tops the charts, gets blocked by Amazon and reveals a serious flaw
items.texteHtml: Muse, Meta's new consumer assistant, drew more downloads and daily active users in the United States and Canada than ChatGPT over the same period after its mobile launch, according to Appfigures estimates cited by TechCrunch. The success hit a wall: Amazon cut off Muse's access to its pages, with a message warning that "continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon's terms of service", The Verge reports. Meta had not warned Amazon that its agent was coming. At the same time, Ars Technica describes a serious zero-day flaw: a simple ClickFix-style attack is enough to hijack this assistant, which the outlet calls "extraordinarily privileged", able to act on the user's behalf. The three-part story sums up the moment: an agent that wins users fast, acts broadly and exposes as much as it helps.

items.titre: British Columbia sues OpenAI after a mass shooting
items.texteHtml: The Canadian province filed a complaint in California against OpenAI, claiming the company could have used ChatGPT conversation logs to alert police and prevent the Tumbler Ridge shooting in February, Bloomberg reports. The attack had killed nine people, including the person behind the tragedy. The grievance fits in one sentence: failing to report threats made on the platform to law enforcement. The case opens new legal ground, that of an AI provider's liability for the danger signals passing through its service. It will weigh on how providers monitor, retain and pass on what users write to their models.

items.titre: The United States and China agree on a dedicated AI warning channel ahead of the Trump-Xi summit
items.texteHtml: The two countries agreed to open an official dialogue on artificial intelligence, paired with a mutual notification mechanism in case of an incident threatening national security, Wired reports. The agreement emerged from eight hours of negotiations in New York between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, days before Xi Jinping's visit to Washington. Analysts cited by the South China Morning Post see it as a pragmatic step toward crisis prevention, tempered by deep divisions over chip access, model distillation and market dominance. The channel now exists; its effectiveness will depend on what each side agrees to signal to the other.

items.titre: Alibaba unveils its most powerful AI chip, Tencent releases its best image model the same day
items.texteHtml: Alibaba presented what it describes as the highest-performing AI accelerator designed in China, meant to rival Nvidia and to support a massive data-centre rollout of up to 20 gigawatts of capacity by 2032, Bloomberg reports. For scale, 20 gigawatts is close to the output of some twenty nuclear reactors running at full power. The same day, at the opening of Alibaba's AI conference, Tencent launched its most advanced image-generation model to catch up with ByteDance and Alibaba. The two announcements, timed together, signal a Chinese industry pushing its own hardware and software stack while US semiconductor restrictions remain in force. The question of chip exports hangs over this week's Trump-Xi summit.

items.titre: Moonshot's Kimi K3 model lands on Amazon Bedrock, a real-world test for Chinese open source
items.texteHtml: Chinese start-up Moonshot AI has begun supplying its flagship Kimi K3 model to Amazon Web Services, one of the world's largest cloud hosts, the South China Morning Post reports. The model is now available on Amazon Bedrock, AWS's tool for building generative AI applications, presented by Amazon as "a powerful new option for code and knowledge work". The stakes go beyond mere listing: it is a test case for whether open-weight models (which you can download and run yourself) can generate revenue through third-party platforms. A Chinese model distributed by a US cloud giant blurs the usual dividing line between the two ecosystems.

items.titre: When AIs grade AIs, scientific judgement collapses
items.texteHtml: A team shows that automated peer review becomes dangerous as soon as it loops back on itself: as AI-generated reviews enter training corpora, later models learn from judgements produced by earlier ones. Starting from Llama 3.1 8B, fine-tuned on real reviews from the ICLR conference between 2018 and 2023, the researchers trained four successor models on 2024 data and observed a decline in discernment, which they call a collapse of scientific judgement. The authors propose ways to slow the spiral. The lesson holds beyond research: handing an AI the task of evaluating another AI's work, without human oversight, gradually impoverishes the measure of quality.

items.titre: NewsGuard launches a news assistant that draws only on verified sources
items.texteHtml: The US specialist in rating news sites unveils an AI tool limited to 12,000 vetted sources and returning half its revenue to the outlets it cites, La Tribune reports.

items.titre: Suno, target of a new Sony and Universal lawsuit despite its pursuit of deals
items.texteHtml: The AI music-generation start-up, which had unveiled its v6 model on 9 September alongside industry representatives, is now the target of a new action by the two majors, Next.ink reports.

analyse.titre: Amazon blocked Meta's Muse agent, Walmart quietly pulled its ChatGPT integration and retailers are rushing to build their own agents, while 31% of shoppers already prepare a purchase with AI: the moment of advice leaves the brand's own site for the model's answer, and the skill that gains value for a French marketing team is becoming the exact source that ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini cite, by fixing product data and measuring its share of citations rather than its rank in Google alone.
analyse.these: Amazon blocked Meta's Muse agent and Walmart quietly pulled its ChatGPT integration. Both moves say the same thing, and it speaks directly to French marketing teams: the moment of recommendation, when a customer decides what to buy, leaves the brand's own site for the model's answer. The Journal du Net puts it plainly: the brand keeps its content but loses the monopoly on the staging. It becomes a source that ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini cite or ignore, like any other. The numbers show where the shift stands. According to a survey relayed by ZDNet, 31% of online shoppers already use generative AI to prepare a purchase, while the traffic sent by autonomous agents rarely exceeds 1%. The gap draws the roadmap. Advice runs through AI long before the agent clicks in your place. Visibility in the answer is won today; automated buying will come next, and its plumbing is not yet laid, as shown by the doors that Amazon, Meta and Walmart are closing. The skill that gains value in a French organisation then changes in nature. Take your ten best-selling products. Ask ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini the question a customer would ask before buying, and read the answer. Look at whether your brand is cited, whether the price and specifications are accurate, which source the model opens. Where the information is wrong or missing, the cause almost always lies in poorly structured product data and unverifiable claims on your own pages. Fix the data at the source, not the campaign. Measure your share of citations in the models' answers, as you track your position in Google. The shelf has moved into the sentence the machine generates. The brand absent from that sentence no longer exists at the instant the customer chooses. Yesterday's search optimisation aimed at a results page; the one coming aims at a generated answer, and that answer is won through the accuracy of what you publish about yourself. The Masteria editorial team.
